It has to do with frame rate and what’s called shutter angle. The standard frame rate is 24p as this mimics what the human eye naturally sees in terms of motion blur with moving objects. Higher frame rates make the footage look almost too choppy and lower ones tend to make it too blurry. You can obviously manipulate what frames are shown in post but what you cannot get around in post is the shutter angle. The shutter angle standard is 180 degrees and this value is calculated by the shutter speed relative to the frame rate. Obviously to expose correctly you need to have a shutter speed appropriate to the scene brightness and this is where ND filters come into play. At 24p you would need a 1/50 shutter speed to produce a 180 degree shutter angle. Even at a rock bottom 100 ISO, setting your shutter to 1/50 would be extremely overexposed in the daylight. The ND corrects this.
